blocks.text: Propositional logic is a basic form of logic used in computer science. It deals with statements that can be true or false; these statements are called propositions (Fig 2.3).

blocks.alt: Four statements, each with an arrow to its truth value: 2 + 3 = 5 is True, The sky is blue is True, 1 > 3 is False, Today is Sunday is False.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.3: Propositional Logic Statements (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.3).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Propositional logic is the simplest type of logic, but it forms the base of all computer reasoning.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.text: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false; it cannot be both at the same time.

Questions and commands are not propositions. For example, 'The sun rises in the east' is a proposition. A proposition must have a clear meaning and should not be confusing. Propositions are the basic units of logic and are used to form logical expressions. A proposition is usually represented by a capital letter such as P, Q or R; for example, P = 'The sky is blue'.

A simple proposition contains only one statement and cannot be broken into smaller parts, for example 'It is raining'. A compound proposition is formed by joining two or more simple propositions with logical connectives, for example 'It is raining and it is cold'. Compound propositions can express complex ideas and are common in logical reasoning.

Logical connectives join propositions. AND is true when both statements are true; OR is true when at least one statement is true; NOT reverses the truth of a statement (Fig 2.4). Connectives form compound propositions, are commonly used in computer programs, and help in decision making.

blocks.alt: Three rows. AND: circles A and B, an arrow headed A and B, True if both A and B are true, and a Venn diagram with only the overlap shaded. OR: circles A and B, an arrow headed A or B, True if A or B is true (or both), and a Venn diagram with both circles shaded. NOT: circle A, an arrow headed Not A, True if A is false, and circle A struck through.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.4: Logical Connectives (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.4).
